disposition_reason: Cohort biomarker study relating infant urinary arsenic species to apple product intake from food diaries; no apple or food concentrations were measured, and apple juice values in the discussion are quoted from FDA and Consumer Reports.

study.design: Cross-sectional analysis within the New Hampshire Birth Cohort Study (urinary arsenic vs three-day food diary)

period.as_reported: Infants reaching one year of age during 2013 to 2016

study.method: Urinary arsenic speciation by HPLC-ICP-MS (Agilent 8900); tap water total As by ICP-MS
lod: Urinary species LOD 0.06-0.10 µg/L; water LOD 0.04 µg/L

controls.control: exclusive apple product consumption (juice, puree, whole fruit, mixed products)
controls.comparator: infants eating no apple products (n=59, geometric mean urinary sum As 2.78 µg/L)
controls.outcome: Geometric mean urinary sum As 2.38 (juice, n=30), 2.46 (puree, n=67), 2.28 (whole fruit, n=20), 2.73 µg/L (mixed, n=21); no significant association with apple intake

unresolved: Urine is a biological matrix, not a food result; no food concentrations were extracted.
Apple juice survey values in the discussion are quoted from FDA and Consumer Reports and were not extracted.

regulatory_or_exposure.what: FDA proposed action level for inorganic arsenic in apple juice, as cited

source_record_corrections: The PDF is the HHS Public Access author manuscript (PMC), not the publisher version; it gives the final citation Expo Health 2020 Dec;12(4):561-567, doi:10.1007/s12403-020-00356-7.
